Configuration lives in `oasts.yaml`, `oasts.json`, or a typed `oasts.config.ts`.
The YAML and JSON forms are validated against a published JSON Schema, so a typo fails with a rule ID rather than silently doing nothing.
Unknown keys are rejected.
Point `$schema` at it for editor completion — oasts validates it as a URI and otherwise ignores it:

```yaml
$schema: https://example.com/oasts.schema.json
```

Paths inside the file resolve relative to `workspaceRoot` (see below), not your working directory.
See [CLI](/reference/cli#config-discovery) for how the file is found.

```yaml title="oasts.yaml"
schemaVersion: 1
input:
  path: ./openapi.yaml
output: ./generated
artifacts:
  types: true
  client: true
client:
  authEnforcement: types
  baseUrl:
    source: server
    index: 0
validation:
  engine: off
  unchecked: allow
```

Three keys are required: `schemaVersion` (always `1`), `input`, and `output`.

Examples on this page pin their values rather than showing defaults — the example above asks for `baseUrl.source: server` and `unchecked: allow` because it is making those choices, not because they are what you get by leaving them out.
The prose under each section below gives the real default.

## `workspaceRoot`

`input`, `output`, and `typescript.tsconfig` all resolve relative to `workspaceRoot`, not directly to the config file.
It defaults to `.` — the config file's own directory — so leaving it out means "relative to the config file" is exactly right:

```yaml
workspaceRoot: .
```

`local.allowPaths` is the one path that always resolves against the config file's directory, regardless of `workspaceRoot`.

## `input`

Exactly one of a local path or an HTTP(S) URL.

```yaml
input:
  path: ./openapi.yaml
```

`input.url` names a document to retrieve over HTTP(S). Naming one is not enough on its own:

```yaml title="oasts.yaml"
schemaVersion: 1
input:
  url: https://api.example.com/openapi.yaml
output: ./generated
```

That config is refused with `error[OASTS2021]: retrieving 'https://api.example.com/openapi.yaml' is not authorized: 'api.example.com' is not listed in remote.allowHosts`, and nothing is requested.
Retrieval needs the host authorized and the bytes pinned, both under [`remote`](#remote).

An `https://` `$id` inside the document is a different thing entirely: `$id` names a schema resource, it is not a request to retrieve one.
A `$ref` naming a resource the document already declares is answered from the document, and no request is made.

It is not inert, though.
`$id` re-bases every relative `$ref` beneath it, so a sibling `$ref: "./tag.yaml"` that resolves to a local file today resolves to `https://…/tag.yaml` once you add an `https://` `$id` above it — and then it does have to be retrieved.
Same for a `#/components/…` pointer written inside an `$id`'d schema: it resolves against that resource, not the document root.
If adding an `$id` broke a `$ref` that worked before, this is why.

Such a `$ref` is refused with `OASTS2021` unless `remote` authorizes and pins it, so adding retrieval to this compiler did not make any document that used to compile offline start making requests.

## `output`, `namespace`

`output` is the directory everything is written under.
`namespace` defaults to `api` and names the aggregate client file (`client/api.ts` — see `aggregate` below) and the TanStack query-key namespace.
It's also what will prefix the emitted module namespace once more than one API can be generated into one tree.

## `artifacts`

Each artifact is a boolean, or a block:

```yaml
artifacts:
  types: true
  client: true
  zod: false
  validators: false
  tanstack: false
  msw: false
validation:
  engine: "off"
  unchecked: allow
```

The client artifact requires an explicit `validation` block; `engine: "off"` opts out of boundary checking.
See [`validation`](#validation) below.

```yaml
artifacts:
  types:
    enabled: true
    directory: shared/model
  client:
    directory: sdk/fetch
emit:
  runtimeDirectory: shared/kernel
```

Each artifact lands in its own directory under `output`, named after the artifact by default.
Rename or nest any of them and the imports between artifacts follow.
Two enabled artifacts may not share a directory, or nest one inside another — that is an `OASTS0102` at config time rather than a collision at write time.

With no `artifacts` block you get types.

Every block below is a fragment, not a whole config.
Options for an artifact you have not enabled are an error, not a no-op — a `zod:` block without `artifacts.zod` is an `OASTS0121`, and a `validation:` block without `artifacts.client` is an `OASTS0161`.
Enable the artifact first, then configure it.

## `types`

```yaml
types:
  enum: literal          # literal | const
  enumExtensions: accept # accept | reject
  dateTime: string       # string | date | temporal
  date: string           # string | temporal
  discriminatedUnions: structural   # structural | tagged
  integer: number        # number | bigint
  readonly: false
```

`discriminatedUnions: tagged` intersects each branch of a `discriminator` union with its own mapping literal so TypeScript can narrow on the tag; `integer: bigint` maps `format: int64` to `bigint`.
Both are covered in [Types](/artifacts/types#shape-knobs).
`enum: const` and `readonly: true` are covered there too — see [Enum representation](/artifacts/types#enum-representation) and [Readonly](/artifacts/types#readonly).
`dateTime` and `date` have their own page — [Dates and times](/guides/dates).

`dateTime: date`, `dateTime: temporal`, `date: temporal` and `integer: bigint` need the **client** artifact: the conversion between the wire form and the TypeScript type lives in the client runtime, so each is an `OASTS0131` on a types-only build.
`enum`, `discriminatedUnions`, `readonly` and `enumExtensions` are types-only shape knobs — none of them need the client artifact.
`integer: bigint` additionally rules out the tanstack artifact, whose query keys are JSON-serialized and cannot carry a `bigint`.

`enumExtensions: reject` turns the vendor extensions `x-enum-varnames`, `x-enumNames`, `x-enum-descriptions` and `x-enumDescriptions` into a build error instead of honoring them; `accept` (the default) uses them to name and describe enum members.

## `client`

```yaml
client:
  authEnforcement: types    # types | runtime
  aggregate: false
  baseUrl:
    source: runtime         # runtime | server | literal
  fetchOptions: {}          # every key below is unset unless you set it
    # credentials: omit | same-origin | include
    # cache: default | no-store | reload | no-cache | force-cache | only-if-cached
    # redirect: follow | error | manual
    # referrerPolicy: no-referrer | no-referrer-when-downgrade | same-origin | origin |
    #   strict-origin | origin-when-cross-origin | strict-origin-when-cross-origin | unsafe-url
    # mode: cors | no-cors | same-origin
    # keepalive: false
```

Fetch is the only client implementation today, so there is no `client.transport` selector.

- **`baseUrl.source: runtime`** — the caller supplies it when constructing the transport, and the generated `TransportConfig` requires it. This is the default.
- **`baseUrl.source: server`** — take the document's `servers[index]`.
- **`baseUrl.source: literal`** — a `value` you write here.
- **`authEnforcement`** — `types` puts security requirements in the call signature; `runtime` moves the check to call time. See [Auth](/guides/auth#compile-time-or-call-time).
- **`aggregate`** — also re-export every operation from `generated/client/api.ts`. Off by default, because the aggregate names every operation and a bundler cannot drop the ones you never call.
- **`fetchOptions`** — static defaults baked into every operation descriptor. Nothing is baked in until you set a key yourself. See [Transport](/guides/transport#static-fetch-defaults).

## `validation`

```yaml
validation:
  engine: "off"      # off | zod | generated — required, no default
  request: false
  response: false
  unchecked: warn    # warn | error | allow
```

With the client artifact enabled the whole block is required, and `engine` has no default — the choice is always written down.
The rest has to agree with it: `"off"` needs `request` and `response` both `false`, any other engine needs at least one of them `true`, `zod` needs `artifacts.zod`, and `generated` needs `artifacts.validators`.

`unchecked` is the policy for successful response data the document declares no schema for.
It is settled at generation rather than at runtime: `allow` accepts it, `warn` (the default) prints a warning and continues, and `error` refuses to build.
`error` only makes sense alongside `response: true`.
See [Validation](/artifacts/validation).

## `zod`

```yaml
zod:
  flavor: classic    # classic | mini
```

## `filters`

Narrows what gets generated.
Each axis takes `include` and `exclude` pattern lists; a pattern is exact string equality or a slash-delimited regex that must match the **whole** subject, with an optional trailing `i` flag.
Exclude beats include.

```yaml
filters:
  tags:
    include: [pets]
  operations:
    exclude: [deletePet]
  paths:
    include: ["/^\\/pets\\/.*/"]
  methods:
    exclude: ["/^(trace|options)$/i"]
  deprecated: true    # keep deprecated operations
  orphans: false      # drop component schemas nothing reaches
```

A pattern that matches nothing fails the build with an `OASTS0262` rather than quietly shrinking your client.
See [Generating a slice](/guides/filters).

## `naming`

```yaml
naming:
  fileCase: kebab          # kebab | snake | camel | pascal | preserve
  typeCase: pascal         # pinned
  propertyCase: preserve   # pinned
  operationCase: camel     # camel | preserve
  enumMemberCase: pascal   # pascal | camel | screamingSnake | preserve
  typePrefix: ""
  typeSuffix: ""
  overrides:
    schemas: {}
    schemasBySource: {}
    operations: {}
    webhooks: {}
    callbacks: {}
    pathSegments: {}
```

`typeCase` accepts only `pascal` and `propertyCase` only `preserve` — property names are wire names.
See [Naming](/guides/naming).

## `documentation`

TSDoc derived from the document. All on by default:

```yaml
documentation:
  enabled: true
  summary: true
  description: true
  deprecated: true
  examples: true
  constraints: true
```

`constraints` is the one worth knowing about: validation-only keywords that cannot appear in the TypeScript type — ranges, patterns, length bounds — are carried into the doc comment instead, so the information is at your cursor even where the type cannot express it.
A `format` the validation artifacts [assert](/artifacts/validation#string-formats) is left out of that list, since the check itself is the record of it.

## `emit`

```yaml
emit:
  runtimeDirectory: runtime
  importExtension: ".js"   # ".js" | "none"
  banner: []
  format: deterministic
```

`banner` prepends lines to every emitted file.
Each entry has to stay one line and stay out of the compiler's way, so a NUL, a line break of any kind, a `sourceMappingURL=`, or the generated-header text itself is an `OASTS0211`.
`importExtension` is what emitted imports end in — `.js` suits Node's ESM resolution and the bundlers that follow it; `none` emits extensionless imports for resolvers that want those instead.

## `typescript`

```yaml
typescript:
  tsconfig: auto     # auto | off | a path relative to workspaceRoot
```

## `limits`

Bounds on the document graph, as a guard against a pathological or hostile input:

```yaml
limits:
  maxDocumentBytes: 33554432     # 32 MiB
  maxTotalBytes: 268435456       # 256 MiB
  maxDocuments: 256
  maxRefDepth: 64
```

Each is clamped to a range, and a value outside it fails the build rather than silently clamping: `maxDocumentBytes` 1 KiB–1 GiB, `maxTotalBytes` 1 KiB–4 GiB, `maxDocuments` 1–4096, `maxRefDepth` 1–1024.

## `local`

The trust boundary for local documents and their `$ref` targets.
Each entry widens the set of directories a local reference may be read from:

```yaml
local:
  allowPaths:
    - ../shared-schemas
```

Entries are resolved relative to the config file and **must be relative** — an absolute path is an `OASTS0221`.
The default is empty, so a document only reaches what the workspace root already covers.

## `remote`

The trust boundary and retrieval policy for documents read over HTTP(S), the way `local` is the boundary for documents read from disk:

```yaml title="oasts.yaml"
remote:
  allowHosts:
    - api.example.com
  allowInsecure: false
  timeoutMs: 30000
  maxRedirects: 3
  integrity:
    "https://api.example.com/openapi.yaml": "sha256:8b4a7f7b1d2c0e5a9f3b6d8c1e4a7f0b3d6c9e2a5f8b1d4c7e0a3f6b9d2c5e8a"
```

Every key defaults to the conservative reading, so a config with no `remote` block retrieves nothing at all.

`allowHosts` is the boundary. It defaults to empty, which authorizes no host, and each entry is a bare host name — a scheme, a port, or a path in an entry is an `OASTS0271`. Matching is on the host alone, so any port on an authorized host is admitted. A URI naming an unlisted host is an `OASTS2021` and no request is made.

`integrity` maps each retrievable URI to the digest of the bytes it must serve, written as `sha256:` and 64 lowercase hex digits — the same rendering as the `Source digest` in every emitted file. There is no unpinned mode:

- A URI with no entry is an `OASTS2022`, refused before anything is requested.
- Bytes that hash to anything else are an `OASTS2023`, and the message prints the digest that *was* served so recording it is a copy rather than a transcription. Fetch once, read the digest out of the diagnostic, paste it in.

That is what keeps [determinism](/concepts/determinism) byte-keyed when the bytes arrive over a network. It also means each URI is pinned on its own: a `$ref` from a retrieved document to another URI needs its own `integrity` entry.

`allowInsecure` defaults to `false`, so only `https` is retrieved and a plain `http` URI is an `OASTS2021`. TLS certificates are always verified against the Mozilla root program; there is no setting that turns that off.

`maxRedirects` defaults to `3` and bounds how many `3xx` hops one retrieval may take. Redirects are not delegated: the compiler resolves each `Location`, checks the host it names against `allowHosts`, and only then makes the next request — so a redirect cannot deliver a document from a host you did not list. Exceeding the budget is an `OASTS2024`.

A retrieved document keeps the URI that was **requested** as its identity, not the one a redirect landed on. Relative `$ref`s inside it therefore resolve against the URI you wrote, which is what makes the compile a function of the URI plus its pinned digest rather than of wherever a redirect points today.

`timeoutMs` defaults to `30000` and bounds each request. Anything the network does wrong — refused connection, DNS failure, timeout, a non-`200` status, a body over `limits.maxDocumentBytes` — is an `OASTS2024` naming the URI and what went wrong. There is no cache and no stale fallback: a build with no network fails, loudly, saying what it could not retrieve.

<Aside type="caution" title="Retrieval is a host capability">
  The [playground](/playground) compiles in your browser, in a WebAssembly module that declares no imports and so cannot make a request at all.
  It refuses a `remote` block while reading the config, and refuses an authorized URI with `OASTS2025`.
  The CLI and the Node package both retrieve normally.
</Aside>

## `compat`

Opt-in departures from strict OpenAPI conformance, for documents describing a server that is itself non-conformant:

```yaml
compat:
  deepObjectEncoding: strict    # strict | extended
```

`strict` admits `deepObject` only where OpenAPI defines it — an `object`-projecting schema.
`extended` admits every schema shape, lowering each with the bracket-path encoding `qs` uses, which is what real documents that declare `deepObject` on arrays are usually describing.

<Aside type="note">
  Add nothing here speculatively.
  Each key exists because a real server disagrees with the specification, and turning one on means the generated client stops matching what your document literally says.
</Aside>

## Reserved keys

`specs`, `shared`, `watch` and `ci` are accepted by the schema but not implemented in this build.
They are reserved so a config written today does not have to change shape when they land, and they refuse in the [provisional band](/concepts/diagnostics) rather than as ordinary config errors:

| Key | Code |
| --- | --- |
| `specs`, `shared` | `OASTS9002` — workspace configs |
| `watch`, `ci` | `OASTS9003` — the surrounding capability |

The CLI has the same arrangement: `oasts watch` parses and then refuses with `OASTS9004`, and `--spec` refuses with the same `OASTS9002` the `specs` key does.
Both exit `2`.
See [CLI](/reference/cli).
